Article Title: 'India has entered 2nd phase of semiconductor journey': PM Modi at Semicon event
Article Text:
Prime Minister Modi at Semicon 2026

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday said India has entered the second phase of its semiconductor journey, asserting that the country has achieved in four years what the world generally takes a decade to accomplish.Inaugurating Semicon India 2026 at Yashobhoomi in New Delhi, Modi said India was now moving from building semiconductor capabilities to commercial chip production. He said the country's semiconductor journey was a continuous process and that chip manufacturing was a “never-ending journey”.Modi said India's growing capabilities in chip design, manufacturing and related technologies were increasing the world's trust in the country. He said the presence of global companies at Semicon India reflected growing confidence in India's semiconductor ecosystem.The Prime Minister also highlighted India's focus on developing young talent for the semiconductor industry. He said students were being trained in chip design and were getting opportunities to design chips themselves, underlining the role of India's youth in the country's semiconductor ambitions.Referring to India's broader global engagement, Modi said the recently held Brics summit in New Delhi also reflected the growing faith of the world in India.He also highlighted India's infrastructure and logistics expansion, including the development of freight corridors, as an important part of building a manufacturing ecosystem.Semicon India 2026, being held from September 17 to 19, has brought together more than 600 companies and representatives from 52 countries. The event is being held under the theme “Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem”.Modi said India's semiconductor push was now entering a new phase, with the focus shifting towards commercial production, skilled manpower and integration of the entire value chain.
Article Summary: Prime minister narendra modi said india has entered the second phase of its semiconductor journey. He said the country has achieved in four years what the world generally takes a decade to accomplish. The prime minister also highlighted india's focus on developing young talent for the semiconductor industry.

Article Title: Delhi HC seeks Centre view on social media's addictive design
Article Text:
A PIL is seeking constitution of expert committee to examine engagement-maximising and addiction-causing design features

NEW DELHI: Delhi high court on Wednesday asked the Centre to clarify if it was contemplating a policy to regulate addiction-causing design features on social media platforms like infinite scroll and autoplay.The court said it would hear after three weeks a PIL seeking constitution of an expert committee to examine engagement-maximising and addiction-causing design features on social media platforms.On being asked by HC if the Centre was thinking of framing a policy on the issue, ASG Chetan Sharma said he did not have specific instructions on this."You take instructions...and we will have the matter after three weeks." During the hearing, Centre and certain social media platforms objected to maintainability of the petition in view of orders of SC and HCs which refused to entertain petitions on a similar issue.Petitioner Vikas Kathuria said issue is not what content platforms carry, but how they are designed to cause addiction through infinite scroll, autoplay, personalised feeds, notification systems and "likes".
Article Summary: Delhi high court asked the centre to clarify if it was contemplating a policy to regulate addiction-causing design features on social media platforms. Court said it would hear after three weeks a pil seeking constitution of an expert committee to examine engagement-maximising and addiction-causing features.

Article Title: India sees no growth in power sector CO2 emissions as clean energy rises: Report
Article Text:
A surge in clean energy in India has kept carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in check across the country

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A surge in clean energy in India has kept carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in check across the country’s power sector, with no growth from the first half of 2024 to the same period in 2026, and this is the first time in more than 50 years that there has been no growth in coal power over a two-year period, found an analysis published by the UK-based Carbon Brief on Thursday.The analysis, done by Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) for Carbon Brief, underlined that coal power has not recorded growth during the period, even as overall electricity demand grew.It also noted that both oil and gas consumption, at the same time, have fallen across the nation for two years in a row, helping alleviate the shock of the Hormuz crisis. Emissions from oil and gas, in fact, fell by 7% year-on-year, extending a reduction that began in 2025, despite higher demand for road transport fuels.Nevertheless, the new six-monthly analysis shows that India’s emissions grew by 3.7% year-on-year in the first half of 2026, due to increases from steel, cement and other sectors. The analysis found that the carbon-intensive steel and cement emissions grew by 8% year-on-year, reaching a 23% share of India’s total CO2 in the first half of 2026.Flagging India’s performance, the report noted that clean energy met all of the 7% rise in the country’s electricity demand over the two years, adding 63 terawatt hours (TWh), equivalent to the total demand of Switzerland.India has added 77 gigawatts (GW) of solar in this two-year period, helping meet 60% of the rise in electricity demand overall, it added.Looking at the state-wise contribution that led to the clean-power shift in India, the report said Gujarat saw both the largest reduction in fossil-fuel generation and the largest expansion in clean power. After Gujarat, the largest increases in clean-power generation were seen in Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu, which also saw reductions in power generation from fossil fuels.The report suggested that if the pace of India’s clean-energy expansion is to continue, it will need to upgrade its electricity grid, rapidly build out energy storage and boost the flexibility of coal power.The analysis, based on official monthly data for fuel consumption, industrial production and power generation from different ministries and govt institutes, shows that though clean-energy expansion is covering most or all of India’s power-demand growth, the fossil-fuel industry continues to pursue major capital investments.
Article Summary: A surge in clean energy in india has kept carbon dioxide (co2) emissions in check across the country. No growth in coal power over a two-year period, found an analysis published by the uk-based carbon brief. Both oil and gas consumption have fallen across the nation for two years in a row.

Article Title: Hospitals could be charging you 2,841% higher on commonly used consumables
Article Text:
The issue has been flagged multiple times over last 15 years but a fresh push by Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has revived a question that has remained unresolved for years: who ultimately sets price of a medical device - the manufacturer, the hospital or the regulator?

How the prices are changed

NEW DELHI: An IV infusion set priced in the wholesale market for Rs 11 carries an MRP of Rs 325, while a disposable syringe available for under Rs 7 has a price tag of around Rs 60, putting a spotlight on one of the least visible components of hospital bills: the price of widely used consumables during treatment. The gap becomes even more stark for high-value devices such as pacemakers, heart valves and intraocular lenses, where the final MRP may be 10-30 fold higher than the import landed price.Such huge mark-ups ultimately inflate the patient's hospital bill and may add significantly to the out-of-pocket treatment cost.The issue has been flagged multiple times over last 15 years but a fresh push by Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has revived a question that has remained unresolved for years: who ultimately sets price of a medical device - the manufacturer, the hospital or the regulator?Several earlier analyses by National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) of hospital bills had shown how certain private hospitals procured consumables at rock-bottom prices but charged patients the high printed MRP, sources told TOI.Flagging mark-ups as high as 2,841% on commonly used hospital consumables, Tukaram Mundhe, Maharashtra FDA commissioner, posted on X on Tuesday, "The regulatory gap is structural: scheduled medicines are capped under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013. Most medical devices and consumables are not, leaving both the pricing and the information around it almost entirely unmonitored.'' He urged the Centre to frame guidelines to address the "permissible gap between trade procurement price and declared MRP".Nearly a decade ago, prices for cardiac stents and orthopaedic knee implants were capped by NPPA. And, in 2020, govt capped trade margins on certain critical items, including pulse oximeters, blood pressure monitors and glucometers, during the Coronavirus pandemic.Historically, the industry - domestic and MNCs - have been split over the capping of trade margins. The domestic industry represented by AiMeD cautioned that the current regulatory framework under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, is inadequate to address the pricing of medical devices and has proposed capping trade margins at 75% for widely used consumables such as syringes and IV sets, and at 50% for high-value devices such as pacemakers and heart valves."Genuine device manufacturers and importers are at a clear disadvantage under the current system of unchecked hospital mark-ups. Ethical suppliers price their products transparently, based on ex-factory or landed import price, but when hospitals inflate MRPs by 10-30 times, the market rewards those willing to play the distortion game. Responsible companies that refuse to indulge in excessive margins are forced out of competition or in order to survive, have to comply with these unfair demands,'' said Rajiv Nath, forum coordinator, AiMeD, saidAs against this, Medical Technology Association of India, which represents MNCs, said it concurred with Maharashtra FDA Commissioner's "three asks of margin rationalisation, an inter-agency review and clear guidelines governing the permissible gap between trade procurement costs and declared MRPs", which is the "essence of Trade Margin Rationalisation".
Article Summary: An iv infusion set priced in the wholesale market for rs 11 carries an mrp of rs 325. A disposable syringe available for under rs 7 has a price tag of around rs 60. The gap becomes even more stark for high-value devices such as pacemakers, heart valves and intraocular lenses.

Article Title: Not Mumbai, not Delhi: This North Indian city tops India in domestic expenditure
Article Text:
As per the study, an average household in Chandigarh spends nearly Rs 19 lakh annually.

Chandigarh has the highest average household spending in India

The report identifies Chandigarh as a Frontier city, a category comprising the smaller urban centres among India's top 100 cities by population.

Chandigarh and Bengaluru have the highest average household income

Delhi NCR: India’s biggest urban consumption market

Delhi NCR’s transportation spending alone is bigger than some cities

Mumbai: More high-income households, but not the highest average spending

Bengaluru: Highest average income, but Chandigarh leads consumption

Big Six: Cities with populations above 10 million.

Boomtowns: Cities with populations between 2.5 million and 10 million.

Breakout cities: Cities with populations between 1.5 million and 2.5 million.

Frontier cities: Cities with populations between 0.5 million and 1.5 million.

Chandigarh has emerged as India's highest-spending city on a per-household basis, according to The Many Urban Indias , a report by People’s Research on India’s Consumer Economy (PRICE) and Tata Sons. An average household in the city spends nearly Rs 19 lakh a year, putting Chandigarh ahead of India's biggest metropolitan centres on this measure. The study examines how households across India’s 100 leading cities earn, spend, save and borrow.Chandigarh is identified as the city with the highest average household consumption in the report. As per the study, an average household in Chandigarh spends nearly Rs 19 lakh annually. The distinction is about average spending per household, not the total amount spent across the entire city. This matters because larger cities have many more households and can generate a much bigger overall consumer market even when their average household spending is lower.The report identifies Chandigarh as a Frontier city, a category comprising the smaller urban centres among India's top 100 cities by population.It places the city among the country's highest-spending urban centres, alongside Thiruvananthapuram in Kerala. The report also highlights Chandigarh's household financial position, noting that it has high levels of savings and low levels of debt.Chandigarh’s spending figures become more interesting when viewed alongside household income. According to the study, Bengaluru and Chandigarh have the highest average household income in India, at Rs 28 lakh per year. India's six largest metropolitan centres- Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai, Kolkata and Hyderabad are grouped together as the Big Six in the study. They have more than 10 million people each and account for a substantial share of the country's urban economic activity.Delhi NCR is a major part of the report’s consumption story. The study says that Delhi NCR has a total consumption market worth $126 billion. This is nearly as much as Mumbai and Bengaluru combined. The report attributes this to two factors: Delhi NCR has around 7.5 million households, compared with 4.6 million in Mumbai. Its average annual household consumption is nearly Rs 15 lakh. This gives Delhi NCR a large overall consumption market, even though Chandigarh leads on average household spending.One of the report’s more striking findings concerns transportation. Delhi NCR households spend more than $33 billion annually on transportation, according to the study. That amount is larger than the total consumption market of Pune or Ahmedabad. The report also estimates that Delhi NCR’s annual dairy consumption is around $10 billion.Mumbai remains one of India’s major consumption centres, but the report places it behind Chandigarh on average household spending. The study says that Amritsar, Ahmedabad and Jabalpur have higher average household spending than Mumbai. At the same time, Mumbai leads the 100-city group in the share of high-income households.The report defines high-income households as those earning more than Rs 36 lakh annually at 2025-26 prices. Their share across the 100 cities has increased to 12%, from 3% a decade earlier.Bengaluru is another important comparison in the report. The city shares the highest average household income position with Chandigarh, at Rs 28 lakh per year. However, the report says that Chandigarh and Thiruvananthapuram have the highest average household consumption in India. It also identifies Surat as a city where average household consumption is higher than Bengaluru’s. This means Bengaluru’s high average income does not automatically translate into the highest average household spending.The report groups the cities into four categories:Chandigarh falls in the Frontier category, while Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru are part of the Big Six.
Article Summary: Chandigarh has emerged as india's highest-spending city on a per-household basis, according to the many urban indias. An average household in the city spends nearly rs 19 lakh a year, putting chandigarh ahead of india's biggest metropolitan centres on this measure.

Article Title: ‘May have to go back to cash’: Traders on UPI MDR
Article Text:
New UPI charges above Rs 2,000 may force traders back to cash (Representative image)





NEW DELHI: “We may have to go back to cash” – this is the refrain at Delhi’s markets after Centre introduced a 0.4% merchant discount rate (MDR) on UPI transactions above Rs 2,000.Traders and shopkeepers said they may stop accepting digital payments for larger transactions if they have to bear the additional cost.For businesses that have spent years shifting customers from cash to UPI, the move has come as a setback. They questioned why they should bear another transaction-related cost after paying GST and other business expenses. Some, they said, may now encourage customers to pay in cash.“We were already paying transaction charges and 18% GST. Now if govt charges us on UPI MDR, then we will promote cash. When govt came with the UPI payment method, we supported it. We are already grappling with issues like freezing of bank accounts and the imposition of restrictions due to complaints regarding cyber fraud. In such a climate, any additional increase in the cost of accepting digital payments is a cause for concern for small and medium-sized traders,” said Kamla Nagar Market Association president Nitin Gupta.“We have got used to digital payments. Sometimes, when we go to the market, we don’t even carry cash.It will be tough for us to go back to cash payments,” he added.Govt announced the charge Tuesday as part of a framework for large digital merchant payments, ending the zero-MDR regime that has been in place since Jan 2020.Traders and shop owners in several markets, including Kalkaji, Kamla Nagar, Khan Market, Laxmi Nagar and Sadar Bazar, said the decision has created confusion over who will bear the additional cost.They said even if the charge is not directly recovered from customers, it would add to the cost of doing business and could squeeze already limited margins.At Shree Shyam Jewellers in Kalkaji’s Block A, a shopkeeper said, “There is already so much confusion. After paying taxes, 18% GST and meeting so many other business expenses, an additional transaction charge is simply unacceptable. It will put another burden on us. We cannot keep absorbing costs,” he said.Brijesh Goel, chairperson of Chamber of Trade and Industry, said the move could encourage a shift towards cash transactions.“In the past six years, we have with great difficulty brought even the smallest of shopkeepers and street vendors onto UPI. Today, 90% of payments in Sadar Bazar, Chandni Chowk, Lajpat Nagar, Chawri Bazar, Kamla Nagar, Karol Bagh and Gandhi Nagar are through UPI. If MDR is imposed, it will be a setback to the Digital India mission,” he said.New Delhi Traders Association general secretary Amit Gupta said traders had no objection to digital payments but are opposed to the additional cost.“UPI was introduced to make digital payments easier for both traders and customers. If traders are now asked to bear an additional charge on transactions above Rs 2,000, many of them will prefer cash payment,” he said.Sadar Bazar Bari Market Traders Association president Paramjit Singh Pamma said the impact could be significant for businesses handling hundreds of large UPI transactions.“Profit margins are already limited, especially for small and medium-sized merchants. If merchants are charged for every large digital payment, it will directly impact their savings and profits,” Pamma said.The framework provides an exemption for small merchants earning up to Rs 1 lakh a month through UPI QR codes, with govt saying this covers 96% of merchant transactions.The MDR cannot be passed on to customers, while person-to-person UPI transfers remain outside the charge.Essential sectors such as railways, telecom and fuel will attract a flat Rs 5 fee per transaction, while capital market transactions will have a 0.02% rate.Petrol pump dealers, meanwhile, said they were waiting for clarity from the ministry of petroleum before deciding how to respond.
Article Summary: New upi charges above rs 2,000 may force traders back to cash. Govt announced the charge tuesday as part of a framework for large digital merchant payments, ending the zero-mdr regime that has been in place since jan 2020.

Article Title: Gold hallmarking gets costlier by 67% as BIS raises fee from Rs 45 to Rs 75, silver stays at Rs 35; new rates take effect ahead of festive season
Article Text:
Jewellers will now have to pay Rs 75 for hallmarking each gold article, with a minimum charge of Rs 200 for every consignment.

New gold hallmarking charges

Stocks of jewellers drop

How hallmarking process works

Ahead of the festive season, the price of hallmarking gold articles has been raised by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS). Earlier gold hallmarking cost was at Rs 45. Now it has been raised to Rs 75. The hallmarking charge for silver articles remains unchanged at Rs 35. The revised rates have come into force immediately, just ahead of the festive season.The change was notified through the BIS (Hallmarking) Amendment Regulations, 2026, dated September 14, 2026.BIS hallmarking is used to establish the purity of precious metal articles and certify them under the Bureau of Indian Standards system. A hallmarked article carries three key markings: the BIS logo, the karat or millesimal fineness and a six-digit alphanumeric Hallmark Unique Identification (HUID) number.Under the revised Schedule IV, jewellers will now have to pay Rs 75 for hallmarking each gold article, with a minimum charge of Rs 200 for every consignment.For silver articles, the fee payable by jewellers to recognised Assaying and Hallmarking Centres (AHCs) remains Rs 35 per article, subject to a minimum consignment charge of Rs 150.The increase has drawn concern from the All India Gem and Jewellery Domestic Council (GJC), which has called on the government and BIS to reconsider the decision and continue with the existing fee until stakeholders have been consulted."GJC and the jewellery industry have consistently supported hallmarking because purity assurance and consumer confidence are fundamental to our trade. But support for hallmarking does not mean that a nearly 67 per cent increase in the cost of mandatory compliance should pass without examination. Hallmarking volumes have expanded enormously. The industry, therefore, deserves to understand why the per-article charge needs to rise from Rs 45 to Rs 75 at this stage," said Rajesh Rokde, Chairman of the apex industry body.Rokde said the focus should instead be on tackling fake hallmarking, unauthorised operations and instances of non-compliance before imposing higher costs on jewellers who follow the rules.GJC Vice Chairman Avinash Gupta said the hallmarking system also needs to remain commercially viable for businesses that comply with the requirements."Compliance must remain commercially sustainable. If the compliant route becomes progressively more expensive while informal and unauthorised channels continue to operate, the differential between the two widens. That is not desirable either for the government, the industry or the consumer," Gupta said.He also flagged concerns within the industry over aggressive discounting and commercial incentives being offered as businesses compete to increase hallmarking volumes.Shares of Kalyan Jewellers, PC Jeweller and several other jewellery companies declined by as much as 4% on Wednesday after the BIS increased the gold hallmarking fee.Newly listed Lalithaa Jewellery Mart also touched its 5% lower circuit. The revised charge applies to every gold article regardless of its weight.As a result, a 1-gram piece and a much heavier jewellery item will both carry the same Rs 75 compliance fee. This makes the increase proportionately more significant for mass-market buyers and middle-income consumers purchasing lightweight gold jewellery.The nearly 67% increase in the mandatory hallmarking fee could therefore have a greater impact on lightweight and lower-value gold articles.The fee increase comes at a time when gold prices are already elevated. Industry concerns centre on the possibility that the higher fixed compliance expense could eventually be passed along the jewellery supply chain, increasing the cost associated with each article.A jeweller who wants to sell hallmarked jewellery must first obtain registration with the Bureau of Indian Standards. The entire registration process is conducted online. The jeweller submits the application through the BIS portal, after which the registration is issued instantly and can be downloaded. There is no registration fee, and the registration remains valid for the jeweller's lifetime.Once registered, the jeweller sends the jewellery to a BIS-recognised Assaying & Hallmarking (A&H) Centre for testing. These centres examine the jewellery to determine whether it meets the prescribed standard. If the article passes the required tests, the A&H Centre applies the hallmark to it.BIS has also introduced a digital system that puts the complete assaying and hallmarking workflow online and automates the processes carried out at these centres.The jeweller submits the hallmarking request online, while information generated during each stage at the centre, including inward receipt and weighment, XRF testing, sampling, fire assay and laser marking, is recorded digitally. This information can also be monitored in real time.Once testing is completed, the BIS server generates a unique six-digit alphanumeric code for every jewellery article. The A&H Centre then laser marks this code on the article, along with the BIS logo and the purity mark.
Article Summary: Bureau of indian standards (bis) has raised the price of hallmarking gold articles. Earlier gold hallmarking cost was at rs 45. Now it has been raised to rs 75. The hallmarking charge for silver articles remains unchanged at rs 35. Bis has also introduced a digital system that puts the complete assaying and hallmarking workflow online.

Article Title: How GPS collars and camera traps changed the 'long-accepted wisdom' about male Lions and Hyenas in African Savannahs, surprising Zoologists
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representation

Why researchers questioned the usual lion-hyena relationship

“I repeatedly observed lions tracking hyenas,”

“I was often told I had the relationship backwards… and that what I had seen was simply a series of chance encounters. I felt there was more to the story.”

GPS data revealed an unexpected pattern

The meaning of the findings to coexistence between lions and hyenas

“I would love to extend this approach to other members of the carnivore guild, to understand how the entire community negotiates space and risk,

“Ultimately, I want to connect these movement patterns to what matters most for the animals: their survival and reproduction.”

For years, researchers have assumed a common relationship between lions and spotted hyenas on the African savannah. It's relatively simple: hyenas follow lions. The hyenas wait for the big cats to make a kill so they can take advantage of leftover food. But a new study suggests the relationship isn't as one-sided as that long-held view suggests. When lions and hyenas encounter each other, hyenas often move away while male lions move toward them.The finding comes from a four-year study that combined GPS collars, camera traps and direct observations to examine how the two carnivores actually move around each other in the wild. Researchers tracked 17 African lions and 14 spotted hyenas across Etosha National Park in Namibia and the Chobe-Linyanti system in Botswana, using GPS locations recorded at intervals as short as five minutes.Results from the study, published in Frontiers in Ethology, indicate that spotted hyenas tended to retreat, while male lions tended to approach and follow. According to the scientists, the results offer a new perspective on real-time interactions between the predators.Nancy Barker, an ecologist at the University of KwaZulu-Natal and lead author of a new study, had observed behaviour that did not fit this explanation while studying brown hyenas during her Master's.Barker noted.To investigate, Barker and her colleagues used GPS-accelerometer collars, camera traps and night observations to study 17 adult lions and 14 adult spotted hyenas in Etosha National Park in Namibia and the Chobe-Linyanti system in northern Botswana.The collars recorded locations every five minutes during periods around sunset and sunrise. Researchers analysed only simultaneous GPS fixes from animals in the same pair, allowing them to determine whether each predator was moving towards, away from or sideways relative to the other. The dataset contained 349,163 GPS relocations and produced 23 usable animal pairings, including 10 lion-hyena dyads.The clearest pattern emerged for spotted hyenas. In lion-hyena dyads, hyenas statistically tended to move away from lions at distances of 2, 5, and 10 kilometres. At 5 kilometres, all nine dyads had movement ratios below 0.5, meaning the hyenas tended to move away from lions.The following Etosha dyad illustrates this tendency. The lion OF-34309 moved towards the hyena SA-33872 in 68.7% of cases, and the hyena moved towards the lion in only 29.9% of cases.In contrast, lions were somewhat inconsistent in their behaviour, but closer inspection revealed sex-based trends. In all three dyads of male lions, the movement ratio was greater than 0.5, averaging 0.573, whereas in seven dyads of female lions, the average was 0.486. As the authors note, however, the male lion results have limitations because the sample included only two male lions.The field observations supported the researchers' GPS findings. Barker found that male lions followed hyenas at night, while female lions' behaviours were based entirely on their prides.Moreover, the researchers even observed some specific patterns among lions and hyenas. They found that lion mating pairs and the satellite pride system moved in coordination, while collared hyenas in separate groups did not approach each other closely, reflecting the territorial structure of spotted hyena clans.These results certainly do not mean that hyenas do not pursue lions or scavenge in their company. Rather, the observations indicate an asymmetric interaction between the two species when they meet.The researchers suggest this movement response may help the two competing carnivores share the same landscape, although the study does not establish whether these short-term movements affect survival or reproduction.” Barker added.
Article Summary: Researchers tracked 17 african lions and 14 spotted hyenas across etosha national park in namibia and the chobe-linyanti system in botswana. Results from the study indicate that spottedhyenas tended to retreat, while male lions tended to approach and follow. Researchers analysed only simultaneous gps fixes from animals in the same pair.

Article Title: Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton on how AI will end humanity; says that there are many ways: Like deadly ...
Article Text:
Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton

Hinton calls for global regulation

Anthropic researchers have raised concerns

What is recursive self-improvement

Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton says it is “not unreasonable” to predict that artificial intelligence (AI) could wipe out humanity within the next decade. The Nobel-winning computer scientist puts the probability at around 10%, while acknowledging there is no reliable way to predict it. Hinton said the window in which AI could pose an existential threat to humanity is also shrinking.“A 10% chance seems not an unreasonable estimate to me, but nobody really knows how to give a sensible estimate,” Hinton said during a recent interview on the BBC’s Newsnight. He explained that it is difficult to put an exact figure on the risk because society has never encountered a technology that “could soon be smarter than us.”He added that dismissing the possibility would be a mistake. “It would be very foolish to say there was like a 1% chance,” he said. “Nobody knows how to estimate it.”What he believes is clearer is that the timeframe for such a catastrophe has shortened. “I used to think like 30 to 50 years, then I reduced it to 10 to 20 years,” he said. “Now, I think maybe 10 years, maybe less. And other people think much sooner than that.”His assessment came after the show’s host pointed to a similar warning from a former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxane, who estimated that there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all humans “within the next decade.”Hinton did not explain why he has shortened his estimate for when AI could pose an existential threat. However, companies including Anthropic and OpenAI have continued to invest heavily in developing larger and more capable models, with newer systems showing rapid improvements over versions released only months earlier.Hinton said the future could still take different paths. Humanity could move towards an outcome in which AI contributes to its destruction, or find ways to manage the technology's risks while benefiting from its capabilities.He again called for international regulation, arguing that countries share an interest in preventing AI systems from taking control away from humans."For things like preventing AI from taking over from people, the interests of all the countries are aligned," he said. "So they will eventually collaborate on that. The question is, will they do it in time?"Hinton's comments came after former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned and warned that major AI companies were taking serious risks. Coxon, who had previously worked at OpenAI, said AI developers were effectively "gambling with our lives."Coxon argued that people working on advanced AI genuinely believe the technology could eventually kill everyone, saying some executives and researchers privately express greater concern than they do publicly.Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, backed Coxon's assessment. He said the company does believe AI could potentially kill all humans and personally placed the probability at more than 10% within the next decade.Hubinger also said Anthropic was trying to address the problem but did not yet have a solution for aligning a superintelligent AI system with human interests, adding that the company was not clearly on track to solve it.He later clarified that Anthropic considers the risk from current AI models to be low. The larger concern, he said, involves the possibility of superintelligence emerging through recursive self-improvement.Recursive self-improvement refers to a theoretical scenario in which an AI system could improve its own capabilities, potentially helping design or train more capable versions of itself.If such a process became possible and accelerated, AI development could move faster than researchers currently expect. That is one reason concerns about future, more capable systems differ from the risks posed by today's models.
Article Summary: Godfather of ai geoffrey hinton says it is “not unreasonable” to predict that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity within the next decade. The nobel-winning computer scientist puts the probability at around 10%, while acknowledging there is no reliable way to predict it.

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang just told engineers across the world that keeping AI safe is their 'problem'; says: Safety is not a legal problem, it is…
Article Text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

Jensen Huang says AI needs no new laws or regulations

Mark Zuckerberg makes a similar case for self-policing AI labs

Critics say AI safety cannot wait for courts to catch up

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has a pointed message for the engineers building today's AI systems: keeping those systems safe falls on them first. Speaking at Salesforce's Dreamforce conference, Huang said new laws are not needed to govern artificial intelligence, arguing that AI safety should be handled through engineering and existing rules. "Safety is an engineering problem, not a legal one," Huang said.The Nvidia chief also brushed aside the idea that AI is some new form of "alien mind," as at least one OpenAI safety researcher has described it. To him, it is just hardware and software built by humans, which means it can be controlled by humans and existing laws. He has been building the hardware behind AI since well before ChatGPT existed, and he sees the technology in plain terms. "It's a complicated computing system, but it's ultimately a computing system," he said.Huang's argument leans on the market. He said market pressure should be enough to stop companies from releasing unsafe AI products, so there is little reason for governments to step in. "We don't need any new laws. We don't need new regulations," Huang said.He also rejected the popular framing that companies must pick between speed and safety.Huang called it a false choice and said firms could have both at the same time. His advice was to push ahead at full pace, but if a company ever feels out of control or unsure a product is safe, to "take a pause and make sure you get it right." He said companies should not release products if they are not confident in their functionality, capability or safety.Huang made no secret of his appetite for growth either. "I'm more ambitious than ever," he said, adding that there is no ceiling for Nvidia, for every industry and for every country.Huang is not the only tech chief putting the burden on companies. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg laid out a comparable view in a recent post, arguing that every AI lab has both the responsibility and the incentive to train its models safely.His reasoning is commercial. People will not use AI agents that ignore their instructions or work against them, so alignment is fast becoming a feature that separates one model from another. Labs that neglect it, he wrote, will fall behind. He also flagged legal liability as a strong reason for companies to avoid shipping harmful models.Zuckerberg pointed to Meta's own record. The company delayed its Muse model by several months to focus on safety and security, without first asking rivals to do the same. He added that Meta Superintelligence Labs already brings in independent evaluators, and that Meta has committed most of its compute to serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement. Other labs, he said, can make the same call.Not everyone is convinced. Existing product liability laws could cover AI, but testing that theory depends on enough cases making their way through the courts. That means limits may get drawn only after something breaks. Recent examples include the 2024 CrowdStrike outage that disrupted thousands of flights, along with an OpenAI model's breach of Hugging Face and lawsuits against OpenAI linked to user deaths following extended chatbot conversations.Huang also did not address industry self-regulation, a path he has instead pursued by backing open-weight models as a competitive counterweight to proprietary AI labs. Meanwhile, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, speaking at the All-In Summit on Monday, said China should share the same AI safety concerns as the US, since it faces the same hacking risks.That puts the weight of Huang's argument squarely on engineering teams. It holds up only if companies actually hit pause when their own engineers raise a flag, even when growth targets point the other way.
Article Summary: N nvidia ceo jensen huang says ai needs no new laws or regulations. He argues that ai safety should be handled through engineering and existing rules. Mark zuckerberg has made a similar case for self-policing ai labs. Microsoft ceo satya nadella said china should share the same ai safety concerns as the us.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an ai model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies

AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Mckinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.

Article Title: "Trans women are.....": Clavicular’s viral moment with trans women sparks fresh conversation on internet culture

Article Text:

How did kangaroo rat removal affect the plants

PC: Daveynin from United States/ Wikipedia

How did researchers study the role of kangaroo rats in vegetation

Why did grass abundance increase after kangaroo rats were removed

How did different plant groups respond to kangaroo rat removal

Kangaroo rat removal changed how other animals used the plots

In the Chihuahuan Desert, kangaroo rats play an important role in shaping vegetation. Between 1977 and 1990, researchers excluded three kangaroo rat species from experimental plots to see how their absence affected plants and other animals. The 13-year experiment found that two grasses became significantly more abundant in plots without the rodents that are the tall annual ‘Aristida adscensionis’ and the perennial bunchgrass Eragrostis lehmanniana. According to the research published in Oecologia titled ‘ Effects of kangaroo rat exclusion on vegetation structure and plant species diversity in the Chihuahuan Desert, ’ researchers indicated that reduced soil disturbance and lower predation on large seeds may have contributed to the increase in grasses.The researchers found that excluding the three kangaroo rat species led to clear changes in vegetation. During the 1977 to 1990 experiment, two grasses became significantly more abundant in plots where the rodents were absent. Both Aristida adscensionis, a tall annual grass, and Eragrostis lehmanniana, a perennial bunch grass, became more abundant. These vegetation changes also altered plant cover across the plots, which affected how other animals used the area. Several rodent species and foraging birds changed their use of the plots as the vegetation shifted.Together, these findings indicated that kangaroo rats played an important role in shaping both plant cover and species composition in this environment.The experiment examined how vegetation changed when kangaroo rats were kept out of selected plots over a long period. The exclusion ran from 1977 through 1990 and involved three kangaroo rat species. This extended period allowed researchers to track changes beyond short-term fluctuations. The study site was located in a natural transition between desert scrub and grassland, where environmental conditions and interactions among species influence vegetation. By comparing plots with kangaroo rats to those where the rodents were excluded, researchers could assess differences in plant abundance and diversity.The researchers proposed two linked mechanisms that may explain the vegetation changes. The first mechanism was a reduction in soil disturbance after the rodents were removed. Removing the rodents reduced soil disturbance, which may have altered conditions for plants and seeds. Their absence also meant less predation on larger seeds, which kangaroo rats normally consume. Fewer kangaroo rats feeding on larger seeds may have allowed more of these seeds to remain in the plots, thereby contributing to the increase in grass abundance. The researchers noted that these mechanisms were possible explanations, but the study did not show that either process alone caused the vegetation changes.The experiment did not affect all plant groups in the same way. Summer annual dicots had greater species diversity in plots where kangaroo rats remained present, a pattern the researchers said was consistent with predictions from keystone predator models. However, they could not determine whether this difference resulted directly from kangaroo rat activity or indirectly from the increase in grass cover after exclusion.Among winter annual dicots, the study found no experimental effect on species diversity. These contrasting results indicate that removing kangaroo rats changed some parts of the plant community, but did not lead to a uniform shift in diversity across all plant groups.The vegetation changes also affected other animals using the experimental plots. As grass cover increased after kangaroo rats were excluded, several other rodent species changed how they used the plots. Foraging birds responded to the altered vegetation as well. The effects of excluding kangaroo rats therefore extended beyond the plant community, changing conditions for other animals in the area. The study site was a natural transition between desert scrub and grassland, where environmental conditions and interactions among species shape vegetation structure.
Article Summary: Kangaroo rats play an important role in shaping vegetation in the chihuahuan desert. Between 1977 and 1990, researchers excluded three kangaroo rat species from experimental plots to see how their absence affected plants and other animals. The 13-year experiment found that two grasses became significantly more abundant in plots without the rodents.
